'''James P. Pierpont''' (June 16, 1866 &ndash; December 9, 1938) was an [[United States|American]] [[mathematician]] born in Connecticut.{{r|ore|mt}}

==Life==
His father [[Cornelius Pierpont]] was a wealthy [[New Haven]] businessman. He did undergraduate studies at [[Worcester Polytechnic Institute]], initially in mechanical engineering, but turned to mathematics. He went to Europe after graduating in 1886. He studied in [[Berlin]] and later in [[Vienna]].{{r|ore|mt}} He prepared his Ph.D. at the [[University of Vienna]] under [[Leopold Gegenbauer]] and [[Gustav Ritter von Escherich]]. His thesis, defended in 1894, was entitled ''Zur Geschichte der Gleichung fünften Grades bis zum Jahre 1858''.{{r|ore|mt|mg}} After his defense, he returned to New Haven and was appointed as a lecturer at [[Yale University]], where he would spend most of his career. In 1898, he became professor.{{r|ore|mt}}

==Research==
Initially, his research dealt with the [[Galois theory]] of equations.{{r|ore|mt}} The [[Pierpont prime]]s are named after him, as he introduced them in 1895 in connection with a problem of constructing [[regular polygon]]s using [[conic section]]s.{{r|martin}}
After 1900, he worked in real and complex analysis.{{r|ore|mt}}

In his textbooks of [[real analysis]], he introduced a definition of the integral analogous to [[Lebesgue integration]]. His definition was later criticized by [[Maurice Fréchet]].{{r|ore}} In the 1920s, he finally turned his interest to [[non-Euclidean geometry]].{{r|ore|mt}}
